blocks.text: The last verse of the Book of Isaiah offers much of interest from a zoological point of view. It reads: ויצאו וראו בפגרי האנשים הפשעים בי כי תולעתם לא תמות ואשם לא תכבה והיו דראון לכל בשר. According to Rashi, תולעת is the maggot of corpses, and according to Kimchi דראון is identical with דירה (§. 413); but what sense would the phrase "their maggot shall not die" have? Must not the maggot that develops from the remains of the corpses also finally cease along with them? Furthermore, דירה is a dry, sapless insect, which is not the case with that maggot. If we add that Jonathan strikingly renders that phrase by ארי נשמתהון לא ימותון, the question arises how תולע can be explained by נשמה. Pollak's explanation (in the Hebrew Jeschurun, issue 2, p. 61), that Ψυχή [psychē] means butterfly, and that just as the butterfly is enveloped in the chrysalis, so the soul is enveloped in the body, must appear far too artificial. I would read גשמהון for נשמתהון; the human body is elsewhere also called a worm, see Job. 25, 6; Ps. 22, 7; אשם is (according to the explanation of most commentaries) a designation of the soul and thus in our passage the opposite of תולעה, i.e., the body. The sense of our passage is: The wicked, through the horrifying state of their being, will become an abhorrence to all beings. Their soul will not be extinguished and so their body will not die off; they will therefore find themselves in a state of agony. The translation of the verse would therefore be: "People will go out wishing to see the corpses of those wicked men; but their body will not die off, since their soul is not extinguished, and thus they will become an abhorrence to all beings."
כי here has the meaning of contrast, as very frequently elsewhere, and already Kimchi relates תולעת to the body.

While the Talmud (Megilla 18a) states that it does not know the meaning of the biblical אחשתרנים (Ester 8, 10), the word is explained by more recent scholars as couriers (Bensey: Monatsnamen etc. p. 188), or royal messengers (Fürst in the dictionary). The old exegetes take the word as the name of an animal, [p. 365] and we will here merely cite their views.
Rashi (on the biblical passage) says: A kind of swift-running camels.
Ibn Ezra takes the word as the name of mules, foaled by the ass and the mare, which are better than hinnies (§. 168).

In the commentary on the Book of Esther (which consists of excerpts from the commentaries of R. Jos. Kara and R. Sam. b. Meir and was edited by Jellineck [Leipz. 1855]) it says: "In a marginal gloss it was remarked that רכש האחשתרנים are horses with eight feet, which run swiftly." A stately counterpart to the well-known Greek Pegasus.

The Targum translates אחשתרנים by ערטליוני "naked ones," i.e., messengers who lay aside all superfluous garments so that they may make their way as unhindered and swiftly as possible; but perhaps in the sense that the offspring of slave women (בני הרמכים) were employed in the courier service only scantily and half clothed.
Midrasch Jalkut Schimoni part 1, fol. 201a has a reading not found in the Talmud passage Bechoroth 57b, namely: חוירין שבמקומנו יש לה ששים רבוא קלפי עלין

יחוש שבמקומנו יש בו ששים ריבוא קלפים כבית הםםם שלו. The Talmud says nothing of יחוש. We leave it to that marvel of an anatomist who so scrupulously examined and determined the stomach of a gnat; here let attention merely be drawn to the striking variant and to the rare, perhaps erroneous spelling בית המסם for המסם in the Midrash. It should be noted, however, that in the same Midr. part 2, fol. 154b the reading of the Talmud is found unchanged.

The second Targum on the Book of Esther (ch. 1, v. 2) deserves to be called a classic passage, particularly with regard to animal voices, which we dealt with in §. 38. We give its content here, since it is moreover of interest for textual criticism. Solomon's throne had six steps; on the first, facing each other, were the lion and the ox; on the second the sheep (צימרא) and the ריבא (if this reading is correct, the word means: wolf; in the passage cited further below [p. 366] the animal is called דובא and may perhaps also mean bear; cf. Mich. Geiger in the אגרת מלאכת מחשבה p. 19); on the third step the leopard (נימרא, as the commentary פחשנן הכתב read, and which is also correct, as emerges from the passage cited below; in the edition Frankf. a. d. Oder a 5544 stands נשרא, eagle, as Buxdorf Lex. p. 147 also read) and אינקא, which Passegen ha-Ketab translates as camel; Buxdorf takes it for the name of a bird; in the passage cited below the pl. of this name is אנקין. If the reading נימרא or נמרא is the correct one, then אינקא is indeed more probably to be taken as a mammal than as a bird; on the fourth step, facing each other, stood the eagle and the peacock; on the fifth the cat and the cock, and on the sixth the sparrowhawk (בר נצא) and the dove.

Now if, the Targum continues later, a false witness stepped before Solomon's judgment throne, the said animals raised a cry, which is designated differently for the different animals: the oxen געיין, the lions נהמין, the sheep פעיין, the leopards בעיין, the camels בכיין, the cats טיסין, the peacocks מיללין, the cocks מקרקרין; of the wolves and the sparrowhawks it says מחטפין and חטפין (they rushed forward), and of the doves (צפורין) it says, as of the peacock, מיללין.

On the expression בכה for the howling of dogs see p. 24, note *. The word טיסין, which Buxdorf (Lex. p. 865) claims not to be able to explain properly, is the Greek θωύσσειν [thōyssein], which means to bark, buzz, cry etc.
